title: Chapter 143 – Kuang's Stair
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Kuang]

Kuang is fifty-seven years old, and the one thing he has learned about the body is that it keeps a ledger of its own.

It does not lie. A man may lie about his age, his rank, the name of his master, but a spine will tell the truth to anyone who knows where to press. Every winter on the road is written in his knees. Every blow is written in the bones. He can feel them each morning when he wakes, like a long column of figures, and he adds them up, as another man might say his prayers: left shoulder, broken at twenty-two. Three ribs, the year of the Registry. The ankle, the Salt Hands. The back, the avalanche. The total comes out the same every day. He is old, and he is tired, and he is not finished yet.

He is standing on the fifth landing of the Gate stair at the third watch of the night, with his hands on his hips and his breath smoking in the cold, watching a boy try to stand like a mountain.

"Lower," he says. "Your hips, not your shoulders. A mountain does not have shoulders."

"I'm trying." The boy is eleven, thin as a rake, with his hair cropped close to his skull and a blanket still hanging from his neck. He slept for five years. He woke eleven days ago with a stranger's name and a stranger's hands, and nobody in the Sect has been able to make him eat anything but buns. He plants his feet, bends his knees, and wobbles. "It doesn't work."

"It does not work yet. That is a different thing."

"How long does it take?"

"I stood for three years before my master let me move." Kuang scratches his jaw. "Then he made me stand for another three. I hated him. I do not think I have ever been so angry at a person. Then one day I noticed that I could not be knocked over, and I forgot to be angry."

The boy considers this with the grave air of someone who has been given a very large and unwelcome present.

"What is the point?" he says at last. "Standing. When you can just run."

"Ah." Kuang crouches, with a grunt, and the old ledger in his knees adds a line. "Here is a secret, little one. Everyone who runs gets caught. Every single one. Because somewhere there is always a wall." He taps the stone beneath them with his knuckle. "But if you stand, they must come to you. And they must come through you. That is all a stance is. A way of choosing where the wall is."

The boy's eyes go to the dark stair. It runs down below them in a long gray ribbon, step after step, into the cold. He shivers.

"Is there a wall now?"

"Yes."

"Are you it?"

"Today," says Kuang. "For a little while." He stands, and offers his hand. "Come. Time for your buns. And do not tell Qinghe I let you out of bed. She will skin me."

* * *

The Garden has not slept properly in four days.

Everyone feels it. There is a tension in the air like the moment before a thunderstorm, a kind of held breath that makes the children whisper and the dogs lie down in doorways with their ears pressed flat. Kuang feels it too. It sits in the back of his neck, under the old ledger, where an animal feels the first change in the wind.

Jian has gone to Lower Weir. He left at dawn with Pei An and a single pack, to answer the Second House's summons, and he told the family it was only a talk. Kuang watched him go. He has watched that boy go many times. He has watched him walk out of the Garden at sixteen with a bruise on his face and a sword he did not know how to use, and out of the Sect at thirty-six with a charter and a bell, and back again at fifty with gray in his hair and a look that Kuang still has no word for. In all that time he has never once seen him go without something in his hand that looks like a decision.

This time his hand was empty.

"He is going to bargain," Kuang had said, to Feng, on the porch.

"He is going to stall," said Feng. His brother's cheerful face, Kuang noticed, had gone sharp and strange since the fire in the winter. The seam-hearing makes him jumpy. He does not sleep. He sits with his head tilted, as a cat does, listening to something nobody else can hear. "The talk is nothing. Jian knows it is nothing. He wants to see who they send."

"And if they send nobody?"

"Then they are somewhere else."

They look at each other. Neither says the next thing. It is Feng, in the end, who gets up and fetches the old iron lantern from its hook.

"Third watch," he says. "I'll take the Dock. You take the stair."

"The Dock is not mine."

"No." Feng's mouth twists. "But you've the knees for it."

* * *

He has supper in Qinghe's kitchen, because it is the one place in the Garden where nobody asks him anything.

It is a warm low room, with a beam ceiling and a fire and a pot of something bubbling on the hob. Qinghe stands at the table with her sleeves rolled up and a ladle in her fist. She is eighty-two and looks forty-five. She cannot taste a single thing she makes, and she has never once let that affect the seasoning. Little Bell, Yue's youngest, fourteen and still drawing on slates when she thinks nobody is looking, sits on the bench swinging her feet. Wenyuan is asleep in the corner chair with his mittens on his knees.

"Eat," says Qinghe. She sets down a bowl.

"I am not hungry."

"I did not ask if you were hungry."

He eats. It is rice, and pickled radish, and a piece of fish that tastes of salt and smoke and something he cannot name. It is the best thing he has put in his mouth in a month. He tells her so.

"Good." She sits across from him. She does not eat. She watches him with her sharp small eyes. "You are going to do something stupid."

"I am going to stand on a staircase."

"That is what I said."

He smiles. Little Bell holds up her slate. It is a drawing of a very large man with a very small head, planted on a hill, and a row of crooked little stick figures climbing over him like ants. "That's you," she says.

"It is a good likeness."

"Mother says you're the wall."

"Your mother is a wise woman."

"I think you should be a door," says Bell, thoughtfully. "Walls are boring. Doors you can go in and out of." She goes back to her slate.

Qinghe says nothing for a while. Then she reaches over, and, quite deliberately, puts her floury hand on his scarred one.

"When Jian was small," she says, "he would not sleep unless someone sat by the bed. I used to think he was afraid of the dark. He was not. He was afraid someone would go." Her mouth pulls. "You sat by that bed for a month, the winter his fever came. I never thanked you."

"There is no need."

"There is every need. I am old. I may not get another chance." She squeezes, once, hard. "Come back from your staircase."

"I will do what I can."

"That is not an answer."

"No," says Kuang gently. "It is the only one I have."

* * *

On his way up the ridge he stops at the long hall, because he has heard that the Head wishes to see him.

Yan Rongzhi sits propped in a chair beside the window, in a green robe too large for him, with a blanket across his knees and a bowl of gruel on a table at his elbow. He looks up as Kuang comes in. The black eyes go over him slowly, from boots to brow, with the clear dispassionate attention of a man who spent his life judging pupils.

"You are the one they call Kuang."

"Yes, Master."

"You stand like Old Tie."

Kuang freezes. He has not heard that name in twenty years. It is the name of his master, a hard grim man from the northern passes who taught him to stand and died of a winter cough without once having smiled.

"You knew him?"

"He taught my pupils, in the year before I lay down. A very difficult man." The Head's dry lips twitch. "He told me once that the whole art of the body was one lesson, and that no pupil of his had ever learned it all the way."

"What was the lesson?"

"That a stance is not a thing you hold." Yan Rongzhi lifts a thin hand and lets it fall. "It is a thing that holds you. He said that when the stance is finished, the man is finished, and you can tell by the way he looks at the sky."

Kuang is silent for a long moment. He did not know that. He knew a great many things about Old Tie, the man's temper, his cough, the stink of his pipe, but he did not know that.

"Thank you, Master."

"I am an old man," says the Head. "I am allowed to be unhelpfully cryptic." He picks up his spoon. "Go and stand on your stair, Master Kuang. And if you can, look at the sky."

* * *

They come at the fourth watch.

Kuang knows before he hears them. The stone tells him. It is a thing his master called the listening foot, the old trick of standing with your weight on your heels and feeling the vibration of a distant step through the soles of your boots, and on the fifth landing, in the cold, it comes up out of the dark as clear as a drum.

Not footsteps. Feet. Many of them, together, perfectly in time. They are marching up the stair from the Dock, which is impossible, because the Dock is behind the Gate wall and the Gate wall is shut.

"Lan Wen," he says quietly.

The white-eyed man is standing at the rail, where he has been standing for three nights. He has changed since his name came back. He is still tall, still gray, but there is a kind of loose human ease about him now, an awkwardness, as of a man who has been given a new set of hands and is not sure what to do with them. He turns his blind face toward the dark.

"I hear them," he says. "Twelve. No. Thirteen." A pause. "They are not breathing."

"Hollow men."

"Yes. And one that is."

Kuang nods. He has fought hollow men before, at the Sunken Lamp, in a story Ruyan sent. He knows what they are. Bodies with the names taken out of them, walking shells, moved by a single will somewhere behind them. A hollow man does not tire. He does not fear. He does not stop until the will that moves him stops. It is the cruelest weapon he has ever heard of, and it is wearing the faces of the dead.

"Wake the others," he says. "Quietly. Four to the landing. Five on the upper stair. The Unkept hold the rail. Nobody goes past me." He rolls his shoulders. The old ledger adds up. "And send someone to the ridge-house. The Head's people are still weak, but there are a few of them who can swing a pole."

"Master Kuang—"

"Go."

The white-eyed man goes. Kuang stands alone on the stone, in the dark, with the cold in his teeth, and listens to the marching come up the stair. He thinks of Jian, in a gray room at Lower Weir, with a cup of tea going cold in front of him. He thinks of a boy of sixteen with a bruise. He thinks of his master's voice, a long time ago, saying, Stand.

He plants his feet.

* * *

The first of them comes out of the dark like a man walking out of a fog.

He wears the gray of the Registry. His face is smooth and young and perfectly still, and his eyes are the flat eyes of a fish. He carries a short spear. He does not break step as he climbs the last stair, he does not so much as blink, and when Kuang's fist takes him in the center of the chest he goes down like a stuffed sack, with a soft collapsing noise that makes Kuang's stomach turn.

He does not get up.

"Two," says Kuang, to himself. He has hit the next one before it reaches the landing. "Three."

They come in a line, up the narrow stair, one at a time, because the stair is only wide enough for one. That is what he has been counting on. The fifth landing is a stone platform six paces across, with a low parapet on one side and a sheer drop on the other, and the stair above it narrows to a single ledge. A man who stands there must be gotten past. A line of men cannot get around him. They must go through.

He fights the old way. He does not strike for show. He strikes for the joint, the throat, the base of the spine, and each blow is a short hard chop that ends before it has properly begun, because there are thirteen and then fifteen and then, Lan Wen calls from the rail, eighteen, and he has only so many breaths. The hollow men do not shout. They do not curse. They simply come, and he breaks them, and they fall, and the next one steps over the body without looking down.

At the fifth he takes a spear in the thigh. At the eighth a blow on the head that sets bells ringing in his skull. At the eleventh a hand fastens on his wrist and he feels the bones go and sends the thing over the parapet with his other arm, and it falls for a long time in the dark, without a sound.

"Kuang!" It is Feng, from above, with the lantern swinging. "I can hear them. The will. It's up the Dock stair. It's a man. He has a seam through his chest like a doorway. He's using it to move them."

"Where?"

"Behind the last rank. Sixteen steps down."

"Can you reach him?"

"Not with the Dock to guard."

"Then keep it." Kuang spits blood, and wipes his chin. He is, he finds, laughing. It comes out of him in a low rusty wheeze, like air from a bellows. "Keep it. I will fetch him."

* * *

He does not know afterward how long it takes.

An hour. Perhaps two. The lantern goes out. The sky above the stair turns slowly from black to charcoal to the color of dishwater, and the old ledger in his body adds up and adds up and begins, at last, to run out of columns. His left arm hangs. His right leg is wet to the ankle. Something has gone wrong in his side, a hot slow tearing feeling that grows with every breath. Behind him, on the landing, five of the Unkept stand with their backs to the stone. Two are down. Lan Wen holds the rail with a spear in his hands that he does not know how to use, and keeps it going with sheer white-eyed terror.

The hollow men have stopped coming in a line. They are coming in a heap.

"Master!" That is the boy. Kuang does not know how he got here. He is at the foot of the landing, small and white-faced, with a staff in his fists that is twice his height. "Master, you're bleeding."

"Go back."

"I can stand."

"Go. Back."

"I can stand." The boy's voice cracks. He plants his feet. His knees are bent, his hips are low, his small back is straight as a mast, and he is shaking like a leaf. "You said. You said they have to come through."

Something moves in Kuang's chest. It is not pain. He has had a great deal of pain. It is a kind of tightening, as if a hand has closed gently around the old ledger and is turning it over to read the first page.

I stood for three years, he thinks. And I hated him.

"Very well," he says. "Stand behind me. Not beside. Behind." He turns his face to the dark. "And watch how it is done."

He steps off the landing.

He goes down the stair, step by step, with his right arm up and his ribs on fire, and the hollow men part around him like a stream around a stone. He does not strike them. He does not need to. He is walking, and they are falling back, and in the gray light he sees them clearly for the first time: boys. Young men. Faces he has seen in the Registry's registers, in the Court's rolls, in the dead file of the Numbers. Each one is a person. Each one is somebody's son.

"I'm sorry," he says, as he goes. "I'm sorry. I'm sorry."

At the sixteenth step down, in the lee of the wall, he finds the man.

* * *

He is sitting on the stair, with his back against the stone and his legs stretched out in front of him, like a tired traveler resting at an inn. He is in his thirties, lean and neat and bearded, with a veil of gray gauze folded over his forehead, and his hands rest lightly on his knees. In the center of his chest, where the robe has been opened, there is a hole.

It is not a wound. It is an opening, a clean round aperture the width of a man's palm, rimmed in pale light, and through it Kuang can see the stair behind him. A seam. A door. Thin threads of plum-colored light run out from the edges of it, in every direction, down into the dark, to the thirteen men on the stair, each thread fastened to a body at the breastbone like a puppet's string.

"Master Kuang," says the man pleasantly. "I wondered if you would come."

"Who are you?"

"A clerk. Of no importance." He smiles. "The Third of the Second House. The Warden's veil was only a veil. Mine is the seat behind it." A small, courteous movement of the head. "Forgive me. Your friend the Keeper is a clever man. But he has been very careful not to ask what the House did with the names it did not burn."

Kuang stands very still. The blood is running down his leg into his boot.

"You were not going to talk to Jian," he says slowly.

"Oh, yes. We have been talking to him all night." The Third gestures at the opening in his chest. "He is sitting in the Registry hall at Lower Weir at this moment, with a cup of tea, listening to a very persuasive voice describe how the Chain can be safely ended. He is a patient man. He will listen for hours. And while he listens..." The smile widens. "We shall have been up the stair and seated the Gate. By the time he realizes, the Dock will already be ours."

"There's a wall."

"Is there?"

"There is me."

"Ah." The Third looks him up and down: the broken arm, the torn leg, the gray lips. His expression is almost tender. "Forgive me, Master Kuang. You are a good man. I mean that. But you are fifty-seven years old, and you are standing on one leg."

"Yes."

"And you have thirteen of my people between you and the door."

"Yes," says Kuang. "I know."

He takes one step. It is a very small step. It is the first step of the Mountain Stance, the one his master taught him in his third year, and the one Jian learned in the cold yard behind the Garden at the age of sixteen with a split lip and a look of pure hatred. He had never told Jian what it was for. He had never needed to. It is not a technique. It is a promise.

Everything that comes, comes through me.

The Third's smile falters. He starts to rise, one hand moving toward the opening in his chest, and Kuang sees his mistake in the instant it is made. The man is a clerk. He has never been hit by anything he could not predict. He is thinking about the thirteen. He is looking at the left hand, the broken one, because that is the hand that is hanging, and he does not see the right until it is already a hand's breadth from his sternum.

Kuang puts his whole body into it.

Not the arm. The body. The hips, the thigh, the old ledger, every column of it, forty years of standing and all the blows he has ever taken, gathered into one short straight blow that ends where the hole begins. He feels the seam give. It is like breaking ice on a pond. He feels it all the way up to the elbow.

The Third makes a sound. It is not a cry. It is a soft surprised exhalation, the sound of a man who has set down a heavy bag, and the plum-colored threads all go slack at once. On the stair behind him, thirteen hollow men stop in their tracks and sink to the stone one by one, like candles guttering out.

"Oh," says the Third.

And then he is not there.

* * *

Kuang sits down on the step. He does it carefully. He is not certain that he could do it any other way.

The light is coming. The stair is a long gray ribbon running up to the landing, and on the landing there are people, running, shouting, a small figure in front with a staff too big for him. He can hear Lan Wen's high shaking voice calling his name. He can hear Feng on the Dock stair, taking the steps three at a time. He thinks, absently, that Feng is going to fall and break his neck, and he finds that he is smiling.

The tearing feeling in his side has stopped. That is not a good sign. He knows what it means. He has been adding up his body for forty years, and he knows when a column is done.

"Kuang!" That is Feng, arriving. His face is white. His hands are on Kuang's shoulders, then on his ribs, then pulling away red. "No. No, wait. Qinghe's coming, she has the pills—"

"Feng."

"Bai's last batch, there are four—"

"Feng. Sit."

Feng sits. He puts his head in his hands.

Kuang looks at the sky. It is a beautiful morning. He had not expected that. The cloud is breaking in the east, in long rose-colored streaks, and the first light is coming down the stair step by step, as though someone is unrolling a carpet. Somewhere a bird is singing. The air smells of snow.

He thinks about the boy. He thinks about how he will tell him, that the wall was never a thing you do but a thing you are. Then he remembers that he will not be there to tell. That is all right. The boy knows. He saw it. Children always do.

"Tell Jian," he says.

"I'll tell him. Whatever you want."

"Tell him..." He searches for it. It seems to him that there was something. He has carried it for forty years. He has been waiting, as men do, for the right moment, and now it appears that the right moment is this one. "Tell him he held his stance very badly. At sixteen. His left knee was too high."

Feng laughs. It is half a sob.

"And tell him it was the best I ever taught."

"I'll tell him."

"Good." Kuang closes his eyes. The sun is warm on his face. "Good."

Far away, in a room that smells of wood-smoke and onions, a woman is singing a song he half remembers. The words have gone, but he knows the tune. It is the one Qinghe hums while she cooks. He laughs. It is a rich warm ridiculous laugh, a cracked-bell, falling-over-a-chair laugh, the laugh of a man who has stood in the same place for forty years and has just realized that he can finally sit down.

Nobody on the stair hears it.

The ledger is closed.
